title: Ezekiel 2:1–10
context: The voice from 1:28 now speaks. The LORD addresses the prophet as “Son of man,” a title that recurs throughout the book and stresses his human standing before the divine glory. The Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet (2:2). The LORD sends him to the children of Israel, “a nation of rebels” and “a rebellious house” (2:3–7), with the message “This is what the Lord GOD says” (2:4). Whether they hear or refuse, “they will know that there has been a prophet among them” (2:5). The prophet is told not to fear their words or their looks, and not to be rebellious himself (2:6–8). A hand is stretched out with “a scroll of a book”, written within and without, with “lamentations, mourning, and woe” (2:9–10); the eating of it follows in 3:1–3. Later uses of the phrase, such as Daniel 7:13 and in the Gospels, are a different matter and are not the subject here. Both traditions read the commission as shared ground: the prophet’s faithfulness is measured by obedience, not by the response of his hearers.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet, “stand on your feet, and I will speak with you.” Arminian readers note that the one who fell on his face in 1:28 is raised to hear. The title “son of man” reminds him that he is a mortal addressed by the living God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the title “son of man” as emphasizing the prophet’s creaturely weakness before divine majesty. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as gracious condescension, the LORD speaking to a frail human, and neither treats the title as a point of dispute.

verses.text: The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet; and I heard him who spoke to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “The Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and set me on my feet”. Arminian readers see the Spirit’s enabling grace equipping the prophet for his task. Word and Spirit come together, and the prophet is made able to stand and hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Spirit’s sovereign enabling, raising the prophet to receive the word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the Spirit empowering a servant for his office, and both join word and Spirit closely, as the verse itself does.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me even to this very day.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sends the prophet “to a nation of rebels who have rebelled against me”, from the fathers “even to this very day.” Arminian readers note the long history of covenant unfaithfulness. The people’s rebellion is real and culpable, and the LORD still sends a messenger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the depth and persistence of Israel’s rebellion across generations. Shared ground: both traditions read the sending itself as mercy toward a rebellious people, and both see the verse as a sober account of human sin before God.

verses.text: The children are impudent and stiff-hearted. I am sending you to them, and you shall tell them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says.’
verses.arminianNotes: “The children are impudent and stiff-hearted.” The prophet is to say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” Arminian readers note that the message rests on the LORD’s authority, not on the prophet’s persuasiveness or on the hearers’ readiness to receive it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the prophet’s authority grounded wholly in the word he carries. Shared ground: both traditions read the formula “This is what the Lord GOD says” as the heart of the commission, and both note that hard hearts do not cancel the call to speak.

verses.text: They, whether they will hear, or whether they will refuse—for they are a rebellious house—yet they will know that there has been a prophet among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Whether the people hear or refuse, “they will know that there has been a prophet among them.” Arminian readers see a genuine choice set before the people. Their response is real and their own, and the prophet’s presence is a witness either way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s purpose accomplished whatever the response, since the prophet’s word will be vindicated. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as freeing the prophet from measuring success by results, while holding the hearers accountable for their answer.

verses.text: You, son of man, don’t be afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you, and you dwell among scorpions. Don’t be afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet is told again and again not to be afraid, though “briers and thorns are with you, and you dwell among scorpions.” Arminian readers note the honest acknowledgment of hostility. The LORD does not promise ease; he commands courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the command not to fear grounded in the LORD who sends him. Shared ground: both traditions usually read the briers, thorns, and scorpions as images of opposition, and both hear a word of courage for faithful witness under pressure.

verses.text: You shall speak my words to them, whether they will hear or whether they will refuse; for they are most rebellious.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall speak my words to them, whether they will hear or whether they will refuse”. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s task is the same whatever the outcome. The people’s freedom to refuse does not lessen the obligation to speak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the prophet’s duty rests on the command, not on foreseen success, “for they are most rebellious.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as defining faithfulness as obedient speech, leaving the outcome with the LORD and the hearers.

verses.text: But you, son of man, hear what I tell you. Don’t be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth, and eat that which I give you.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t be rebellious like that rebellious house.” Arminian readers note that the prophet himself is addressed as one who could share the people’s rebellion, and the warning is genuine. The command to open his mouth and eat is a test of obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the warning seriously: the messenger is not exempt from the call to obey. Shared ground: both traditions read the command to eat what the LORD gives as obedience before proclamation, with the prophet’s own heart addressed before he addresses others.

verses.text: When I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me; and behold, a scroll of a book was in it.
verses.arminianNotes: A hand is stretched out to the prophet, and “a scroll of a book was in it.” Arminian readers note that the message is given, not invented. The prophet receives his words from outside himself, and the scroll makes that point concrete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that the prophet’s message is received from God. Shared ground: both traditions read the hand and the scroll as a sign within the vision, showing that the word the prophet will speak originates with the LORD.

verses.text: He spread it before me. It was written within and without; and lamentations, mourning, and woe were written in it.
verses.arminianNotes: The scroll was “written within and without”, and “lamentations, mourning, and woe were written in it.” Arminian readers note that the message is often read as full and complete, and it is heavy with grief. The coming judgment is real, and the LORD does not hide it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a complete and sobering message of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the writing on both sides as fullness, and both mention the comparison some draw with the scroll of Revelation 5:1 only in passing.
